blocks.text: The fish, the snake and the pig grow stronger the older they get (A. Sara 30b). Fish flesh gains in flavour through salting, whereas any other meat is indeed preserved by it but does not become tastier (B. batra 74b). Some kinds of salted fish can be eaten without first having to be cooked, such as herrings and anchovies (דגים קטנים, Beza 16a; though, as is well known, there is also smoked salmon and others). Fresh fish taste best (ibid. 24b); by contrast, the dish prepared from fish fat and flour, called כסא דהרסנא (ibid. 16a), loses much of its flavour when it grows old (B. batra 91b). Here [p. 249] the dish is called simply הרסנא, which Samuel renders imprecisely by דגים קטנים, for הרסנא, from הרם, is the pounded part of the fish flesh with which the flour is mixed, and both components of the dish are expressly named קימחא and הרסנא in A. Sara 38a.

For some kinds of fish, being wetted with water after they have been taken out of the water is harmful; cf. the relevant articles on the three kinds of fish named last in the preceding §. According to the Midrash (Rabba Bereschit fol. 7, d), one and the same fish has a different flavour when it is found in different waters; it says there: The flavour of the fish taken from עכו (Acco, i.e. Πτολεμάις [Ptolemais]) is different from that of the one that comes from צידון (Σιδών [Sidōn]) and אספמיא (Spain; see my Aphorisms in the L. Bl. d. Orients 1849, no. 23). The first two Phoenician cities lay on the Mediterranean. The Midrash (ibid. Debarim fol. 298, c) further reports that fish grow fat after the early rain (רביעה); thus a fish caught near עכו after this rain weighed 300 Literas (ליטרא, pounds), which is probably to be understood of its fat, since it says there that (unopened) the fish was estimated at only 4 pounds.

The enormous mass of fish in the waters near עכו also gave rise to the proverb: “Does one bring fish to Acco?” (ibid. Schemoth fol. 126, c); of צידון too it is said (Talm. Schekalim 6, H. 2) that a Rabbi there was served 300 kinds of fish prepared as a single dish.
The Euphrates is called פרת because its water פרין ורבין is very rich in fish (Berachoth 59b). A town in a region rich in fish was called מגדל נונייא “Fish Tower” (Pesachim 46a).
Fish have a sense of smell (§. 351).

The means of catching fish and the receptacles for them are manifold. They were caught either with the hook (איימא, Hameçon), which was fastened somewhere so that one did not even need to be present (Sabbat 18a*), or with nets (מצודה, Menachoth 64a; מצודת הכברין, Kelim 23, 5), or with a net stretched over a hoop and ending in a point, through which the fish cannot pass, and so, in its effort to do so, becomes entangled in the threads by its gill covers (קוקרי, Sabbat 18a).

[p. 250] It was also customary to let the ponds drain, whereby the fish remain behind on the bottom (M. Katan 11a). The drainage ditch is called כוורי (ibid.); finally, fish were also caught with small fishing nets (רושא, Reseau, ibid.).
The fishpond was called ויבייר (Vivier, Beza 23b), the fish tank אקן (Kelim 12, 2) and כוורי (Ketuboth 79a). The fisherman's house built for fishing is called בית הציייר (Nedarim 20b).
On the fishing devices אחלי and אוהרי see Gittin 60b; on חרמים Rabba Bamidbar fol. 229, d.

The chief use of fish lies in the eating of their flesh; the fish juice obtained by salting is also edible (Machschirin 6, 3). From fish fat with an admixture of flour a dish was prepared (§. 311). The eating of small fish was especially recommended. Whoever accustoms himself to eating them seldom gets bellyaches; indeed, eating them even strengthens and preserves health (Berachoth 40a). It is directly prescribed for the sick (A. Sara 29a). Children acquire a pleasing appearance if the mother has accustomed herself to eating large fish during pregnancy (Ketuboth 61a*). After eating fish, water is to be preferred to beer as a drink, and beer to wine (M. Katan 11a). The young fish, however, is not good; only with small mud fish is eating it wholesome; with large ones, on the other hand, the young fish must have reached at least a quarter of the usual size if eating it is not to be harmful (Berachoth 44b).
Fish oil serves for lighting (Sabbat 24b), as does melted fish fat (ibid. 21a). The latter was sometimes mixed with olive oil (Bechoroth 29b).
The skin was used for utensils (Kelim 10, 1) and for writing material (Sabbat 108a).
From the fish bones [p. 251] some implements were made (Kelim 10, 1), and whale bones even served as building materials (B. batra 73b).
Finally, a fish was once used to pull a wagon, while a goat harnessed along with it pulled it along the shore (Sanhedrin 59b).
Fish are tastier some time after being caught than immediately afterwards (M. Katan 11a).
